Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive comparison of the major Next.js authentication libraries in 2026:

## Overview

In 2026, there are three options that dominate new projects: Clerk, Better Auth, and Auth.js v5.

## Key Characteristics

**Better Auth**
Better Auth is a TypeScript-native library that owns your users in your own Postgres with first-class multi-tenancy. Better Auth is a TypeScript authentication library for full-stack frameworks that runs in your app and stores users in your database, and launched in 2024 reaching v1.6 in May 2026. It ships with built-in email/password, OAuth, magic links, two-factor auth, and passkeys out of the box.

**Auth.js v5 (NextAuth)**
NextAuth, now officially called Auth.js v5, is the original Next.js auth library with the same package (next-auth) and same maintainers. Auth.js v5 is the most established open-source option — battle-tested, 40+ provider adapters, and now fully compatible with the Next.js App Router after a significant rewrite.

**Clerk**
Clerk is a hosted authentication service where you add their SDK, get production-quality sign-in screens and user management out of the box, and pay per monthly active user.

## Recommendations

For a new Next.js SaaS in 2026, the right authentication pick is almost always Better Auth or Supabase Auth.

Choose better-auth for new self-hosted TypeScript apps, Clerk when authentication is a product surface you want to outsource, and NextAuth v5 when you are already deep in the Next.js and Auth.js ecosystem and want the familiar path.

## Download Stats

Auth.js has ~2.5M weekly downloads and is the standard Next.js auth library, Clerk has ~300K downloads and is managed auth as a service with $0 for 10K monthly users, and Better Auth has ~100K downloads (fast-growing) and is a newer TypeScript-first alternative to NextAuth with better type safety and plugin system.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Next.js 16 proxy.ts file convention:

## Overview

In Next.js 16, middleware.ts is deprecated and proxy.ts is the new convention. Middleware has been replaced by proxy.ts to clarify network boundary.

## Why the Change?

The reason behind the renaming of middleware is that the term "middleware" can often be confused with Express.js middleware, leading to a misinterpretation of its purpose. Proxy sounds like a network boundary in front of the route, which is much closer to how the feature behaves.

## Migration Steps

To migrate, rename the file from middleware.ts to proxy.ts, rename the named export from middleware to proxy, and update middleware-named configuration flags where they apply. For example, skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize became skipProxyUrlNormalize.

Next.js provides a codemod to migrate from middleware.ts to proxy.ts, which will rename the file and the function name from middleware to proxy.

## File Location

Create a proxy.ts (or .js) file in the project root, or inside src if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as pages or app.

## Functionality

The proxy.js|ts file is used to write Proxy and run code on the server before a request is completed, and based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.

1	---
2	title: proxy.js
3	description: API reference for the proxy.js file.
4	related:
5	  title: Learn more about Proxy
6	  links:
7	    - app/api-reference/functions/next-request
8	    - app/api-reference/functions/next-response
9	---
10	
11	> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.
12	
13	The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.
14	
15	Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.
16	
17	> **Good to know**:
18	>
19	> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
20	>
21	> To pass information from Proxy to your application, use [headers](#setting-headers), [cookies](#using-cookies), [rewrites](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#rewrite), [redirects](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#redirect), or the URL.
22	
23	Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.
24	
25	If you’ve customized [`pageExtensions`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions), for example to `.page.ts` or `.page.js`, name your file `proxy.page.ts` or `proxy.page.js` accordingly.
26	
27	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
28	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
29	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
30	
31	// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
32	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
33	  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
34	}
35	
36	export const config = {
37	  matcher: '/about/:path*',
38	}
39	```
40	
41	```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
42	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
43	
44	// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
45	export function proxy(request) {
46	  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
47	}
48	
49	export const config = {
50	  matcher: '/about/:path*',
51	}
52	```
53	
54	## Exports
55	
56	### Proxy function
57	
58	The file must export a single function, either as a default export or named `proxy`. Note that multiple proxy from the same file are not supported.
59	
60	```js filename="proxy.js"
61	// Example of default export
62	export default function proxy(request) {
63	  // Proxy logic
64	}
65	```
66	
67	### Config object (optional)
68	
69	Optionally, a config object can be exported alongside the Proxy function. This object includes the [matcher](#matcher) to specify paths where the Proxy applies.
70	
71	### Matcher
72	
73	The `matcher` option allows you to target specific paths for the Proxy to run on.
74	
75	Without a `matcher`, Proxy runs on **every request**, including static files (`_next/static`), image optimizations (`_next/image`), and assets in the `public/` folder. Consider using a [negative match pattern](#negative-matching) to exclude these paths, otherwise auth logic or redirects can unintentionally block CSS, JS, or images from loading.
76	
77	You can specify paths in several ways:
78	
79	- For a single path: Directly use a string to define the path, like `'/about'`.
80	- For multiple paths: Use an array to list multiple paths, such as `matcher: ['/about', '/contact']`, which applies the Proxy to both `/about` and `/contact`.
81	
82	```js filename="proxy.js"
83	export const config = {
84	  matcher: ['/about/:path*', '/dashboard/:path*'],
85	}
86	```
87	
88	Additionally, the `matcher` option supports complex path specifications using regular expressions. For example, you can exclude certain paths with a regular expression matcher:
89	
90	```js filename="proxy.js"
91	export const config = {
92	  matcher: [
93	    // Exclude API routes, static files, image optimizations, and .png files
94	    '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|.*\\.png$).*)',
95	  ],
96	}
97	```
98	
99	This enables precise control over which paths to include or exclude.
100	
101	The `matcher` option accepts an array of objects with the following keys:
102	
103	- `source`: The path or pattern used to match the request paths. It can be a string for direct path matching or a pattern for more complex matching.
104	- `locale` (optional): A boolean that, when set to `false`, ignores locale-based routing in path matching.
105	- `has` (optional): Specifies conditions based on the presence of specific request elements such as headers, query parameters, or cookies.
106	- `missing` (optional): Focuses on conditions where certain request elements are absent, like missing headers or cookies.
107	
108	```js filename="proxy.js"
109	export const config = {
110	  matcher: [
111	    {
112	      source: '/api/:path*',
113	      locale: false,
114	      has: [
115	        { type: 'header', key: 'Authorization', value: 'Bearer Token' },
116	        { type: 'query', key: 'userId', value: '123' },
117	      ],
118	      missing: [{ type: 'cookie', key: 'session', value: 'active' }],
119	    },
120	  ],
121	}
122	```
123	
124	The `source` path patterns:
125	
126	1. MUST start with `/`
127	2. Can include named parameters: `/about/:path` matches `/about/a` and `/about/b` but not `/about/a/c`
128	3. Can have modifiers on named parameters (starting with `:`): `/about/:path*` matches `/about/a/b/c` because `*` is _zero or more_. `?` is _zero or one_ and `+` _one or more_
129	4. Can use regular expression enclosed in parenthesis: `/about/(.*)` is the same as `/about/:path*`
130	5. Are anchored to the start of the path: `/about` matches `/about` and `/about/team` but not `/blog/about`
131	
132	Read more details on [path-to-regexp](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp#path-to-regexp-1) documentation.
133	
134	> **Good to know**:
135	>
136	> - The `matcher` values need to be constants so they can be statically analyzed at build-time. Dynamic values such as variables will be ignored.
137	> - For backward compatibility, Next.js always considers `/public` as `/public/index`. Therefore, a matcher of `/public/:path` will match.
138	
139	## Params
140	
141	Next.js calls the Proxy function with two arguments, [`request`](#request) and [`event`](#event), in that order. Declare only the ones you use.
142	
143	### `request`
144	
145	The first parameter is an instance of `NextRequest`, which represents the incoming HTTP request.
146	
147	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
148	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
149	
150	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
151	  // Proxy logic goes here
152	}
153	```
154	
155	```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
156	export function proxy(request) {
157	  // Proxy logic goes here
158	}
159	```
160	
161	### `event`
162	
163	The second parameter is an instance of `NextFetchEvent`. It exposes a single method, `waitUntil(promise)`, which keeps the Proxy invocation alive until the promise settles, so background work like logging or analytics can finish after the response is sent. See [`waitUntil` and `NextFetchEvent`](#waituntil-and-nextfetchevent) for a full example.
164	
165	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
166	import type { NextFetchEvent, NextRequest } from 'next/server'
167	
168	export function proxy(request: NextRequest, event: NextFetchEvent) {
169	  event.waitUntil(
170	    fetch('https://example.com/log', {
171	      method: 'POST',
172	      body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname }),
173	    })
174	  )
175	}
176	```
177	
178	```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
179	export function proxy(request, event) {
180	  event.waitUntil(
181	    fetch('https://example.com/log', {
182	      method: 'POST',
183	      body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname }),
184	    })
185	  )
186	}
187	```
188	
189	### `NextProxy` type
190	
191	If you prefer a shorthand, you can use the `NextProxy` type. It infers the parameter types for both `request` (`NextRequest`) and `event` (`NextFetchEvent`) automatically:
192	
193	```tsx filename="proxy.ts"
194	import type { NextProxy } from 'next/server'
195	
196	export const proxy: NextProxy = (request, event) => {
197	  event.waitUntil(Promise.resolve())
198	  return Response.json({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname })
199	}
200	```
201	
202	> **Good to know**:
203	>
204	> - `NextRequest` is a type that represents incoming HTTP requests in Next.js Proxy, whereas [`NextResponse`](#nextresponse) is a class used to manipulate and send back HTTP responses.
205	
206	## NextResponse
207	
208	The `NextResponse` API allows you to:
209	
210	- `redirect` the incoming request to a different URL
211	- `rewrite` the response by displaying a given URL
212	- Set request headers for API Routes, `getServerSideProps`, and `rewrite` destinations
213	- Set response cookies
214	- Set response headers
215	
216	<AppOnly>
217	
218	To produce a response from Proxy, you can:
219	
220	1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route)) that produces a response
221	2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)
222	
223	> **Good to know**: For redirects, you can also use `Response.redirect` instead of `NextResponse.redirect`.
224	
225	</AppOnly>
226	
227	<PagesOnly>
228	
229	To produce a response from Proxy, you can:
230	
231	1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/pages-and-layouts) or [Edge API Route](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/api-routes)) that produces a response
232	2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)
233	
234	</PagesOnly>
235	
236	## Execution order
237	
238	Proxy will be invoked for **every route in your project**. Given this, it's crucial to use [matchers](#matcher) to precisely target or exclude specific routes. The following is the execution order:
239	
240	1. `headers` from `next.config.js`
241	2. `redirects` from `next.config.js`
242	3. Proxy (`rewrites`, `redirects`, etc.)
243	4. `beforeFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
244	5. Filesystem routes (`public/`, `_next/static/`, `pages/`, `app/`, etc.)
245	6. `afterFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
246	7. Dynamic Routes (`/blog/[slug]`)
247	8. `fallback` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
248	
249	> **Good to know:** [Server Functions](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-server) are not separate routes in this chain. They are handled as POST requests to the route where they are used, so a Proxy matcher that excludes a path will also skip Server Function calls on that path.
250	>
251	> A matcher change or a refactor that moves a Server Function to a different route can silently remove Proxy coverage. Always verify authentication and authorization inside each Server Function rather than relying on Proxy alone. See the [Data Security guide](/docs/app/guides/data-security#authentication-and-authorization) for recommended patterns.
252	
253	## Runtime
254	
255	Proxy defaults to using the Node.js runtime. The [`runtime`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/runtime) config option is not available in Proxy files. Setting the `runtime` config option in Proxy will throw an error.
256	
257	## Advanced Proxy flags
258	
259	In `v13.1` of Next.js two additional flags were introduced for proxy, `skipProxyUrlNormalize` (formerly `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize`) and `skipTrailingSlashRedirect` to handle advanced use cases.
260	
261	`skipTrailingSlashRedirect` disables Next.js redirects for adding or removing trailing slashes. This allows custom handling inside proxy to maintain the trailing slash for some paths but not others, which can make incremental migrations easier.
262	
263	```js filename="next.config.js"
264	module.exports = {
265	  skipTrailingSlashRedirect: true,
266	}
267	```
268	
269	```js filename="proxy.js"
270	const legacyPrefixes = ['/docs', '/blog']
271	
272	export default async function proxy(req) {
273	  const { pathname } = req.nextUrl
274	
275	  if (legacyPrefixes.some((prefix) => pathname.startsWith(prefix))) {
276	    return NextResponse.next()
277	  }
278	
279	  // apply trailing slash handling
280	  if (
281	    !pathname.endsWith('/') &&
282	    !pathname.match(/((?!\.well-known(?:\/.*)?)(?:[^/]+\/)*[^/]+\.\w+)/)
283	  ) {
284	    return NextResponse.redirect(
285	      new URL(`${req.nextUrl.pathname}/`, req.nextUrl)
286	    )
287	  }
288	}
289	```
290	
291	`skipProxyUrlNormalize` allows for disabling the URL normalization in Next.js to make handling direct visits and client-transitions the same. In some advanced cases, this option provides full control by using the original URL.
292	
293	```js filename="next.config.js"
294	module.exports = {
295	  skipProxyUrlNormalize: true,
296	}
297	```
298	
299	```js filename="proxy.js"
300	export default async function proxy(req) {

344	### Using Cookies
345	
346	Cookies are regular headers. On a `Request`, they are stored in the `Cookie` header. On a `Response` they are in the `Set-Cookie` header. Next.js provides a convenient way to access and manipulate these cookies through the `cookies` extension on `NextRequest` and `NextResponse`.
347	
348	1. For incoming requests, `cookies` comes with the following methods: `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete` cookies. You can check for the existence of a cookie with `has` or remove all cookies with `clear`.
349	2. For outgoing responses, `cookies` have the following methods `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete`.
350	
351	```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
352	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
353	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
354	
355	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
356	  // Assume a "Cookie:nextjs=fast" header to be present on the incoming request
357	  // Getting cookies from the request using the `RequestCookies` API
358	  let cookie = request.cookies.get('nextjs')
359	  console.log(cookie) // => { name: 'nextjs', value: 'fast', Path: '/' }
360	  const allCookies = request.cookies.getAll()
361	  console.log(allCookies) // => [{ name: 'nextjs', value: 'fast' }]
362	
363	  request.cookies.has('nextjs') // => true
364	  request.cookies.delete('nextjs')
365	  request.cookies.has('nextjs') // => false
366	
367	  // Setting cookies on the response using the `ResponseCookies` API
368	  const response = NextResponse.next()
369	  response.cookies.set('vercel', 'fast')
370	  response.cookies.set({
371	    name: 'vercel',
372	    value: 'fast',
373	    path: '/',
374	  })
375	  cookie = response.cookies.get('vercel')
376	  console.log(cookie) // => { name: 'vercel', value: 'fast', Path: '/' }
377	  // The outgoing response will have a `Set-Cookie:vercel=fast;path=/` header.
378	
379	  return response
380	}
381	```

420	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
421	
422	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
423	  // Clone the request headers and set a new header `x-hello-from-proxy1`
424	  const requestHeaders = new Headers(request.headers)
425	  requestHeaders.set('x-hello-from-proxy1', 'hello')
426	
427	  // You can also set request headers in NextResponse.next
428	  const response = NextResponse.next({
429	    request: {
430	      // New request headers
431	      headers: requestHeaders,
432	    },
433	  })

436	  response.headers.set('x-hello-from-proxy2', 'hello')

472	#### RSC requests and rewrites
473	
474	During RSC requests, Next.js strips internal Flight headers from the `request` instance in Proxy. For example, headers like `rsc`, `next-router-state-tree`, and `next-router-prefetch` are not exposed through `request.headers`. This is to prevent accidentally handling an RSC request differently than the HTML request as both need to align.
475	
476	When you use `NextResponse.rewrite()`, Next.js automatically propagates the required RSC rewrite headers upstream.
477	
478	If you implement custom rewrite logic with `fetch()` instead of `NextResponse.rewrite()`, you can run into missing RSC headers unless you forward them manually.
479	
480	For custom `fetch` rewrite setups, you can also enable `skipProxyUrlNormalize` in `next.config.js` so your rewrite logic can receive the necessary URL shape and RSC headers from the provided request object:

482	```js filename="next.config.js"

484	  skipProxyUrlNormalize: true,
485	}
486	```

488	### CORS
489	
490	You can set CORS headers in Proxy to allow cross-origin requests, including [simple](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#simple_requests) and [preflighted](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#preflighted_requests) requests.
491	
492	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
493	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
494	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
495	
496	const allowedOrigins = ['https://acme.com', 'https://my-app.org']
497	
498	const corsOptions = {
499	  'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': 'GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS',
500	  'Access-Control-Allow-Headers': 'Content-Type, Authorization',
501	}
502	
503	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
504	  // Check the origin from the request
505	  const origin = request.headers.get('origin') ?? ''
506	  const isAllowedOrigin = allowedOrigins.includes(origin)
507	
508	  // Handle preflighted requests
509	  const isPreflight = request.method === 'OPTIONS'
510	
511	  if (isPreflight) {
512	    const preflightHeaders = {
513	      ...(isAllowedOrigin && { 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': origin }),
514	      ...corsOptions,
515	    }
516	    return NextResponse.json({}, { headers: preflightHeaders })
517	  }
518	
519	  // Handle simple requests
520	  const response = NextResponse.next()
521	
522	  if (isAllowedOrigin) {
523	    response.headers.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin)
524	  }
525	
526	  Object.entries(corsOptions).forEach(([key, value]) => {
527	    response.headers.set(key, value)
528	  })
529	
530	  return response
531	}
532	
533	export const config = {
534	  matcher: '/api/:path*',
535	}
536	```

634	### Negative matching
635	
636	The `matcher` config allows full regex so matching like negative lookaheads or character matching is supported. An example of a negative lookahead to match all except specific paths can be seen here:
637	
638	```js filename="proxy.js"
639	export const config = {
640	  matcher: [
641	    /*
642	     * Match all request paths except for the ones starting with:
643	     * - api (API routes)
644	     * - _next/static (static files)
645	     * - _next/image (image optimization files)
646	     * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
647	     */
648	    '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
649	  ],

706	### `waitUntil` and `NextFetchEvent`
707	
708	The `NextFetchEvent` object extends the native [`FetchEvent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/FetchEvent) object, and includes the [`waitUntil()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/ExtendableEvent/waitUntil) method.

714	import type { NextFetchEvent, NextRequest } from 'next/server'
715	
716	export function proxy(req: NextRequest, event: NextFetchEvent) {
717	  event.waitUntil(

719	      method: 'POST',
720	      body: JSON.stringify({ pathname: req.nextUrl.pathname }),
721	    })
722	  )

725	}

769	## Migration to Proxy
770	
771	### Why the Change
772	
773	The reason behind the renaming of `middleware` is that the term "middleware" can often be confused with Express.js middleware, leading to a misinterpretation of its purpose. Also, Middleware is highly capable, so it may encourage the usage; however, this feature is recommended to be used as a last resort.
774	
775	Next.js is moving forward to provide better APIs with better ergonomics so that developers can achieve their goals without Middleware. This is the reason behind the renaming of `middleware`.
776	
777	### Why "Proxy"
778	
779	The name Proxy clarifies what Middleware is capable of. The term "proxy" implies a network boundary in front of the app, which is how this feature behaves. It can run outside of your application’s main runtime and handle requests before they reach your app. These characteristics align better with the term "proxy" and provide a clearer purpose for the feature.
780	
781	### How to Migrate
782	
783	We recommend users avoid relying on Middleware unless no other options exist. Our goal is to give them APIs with better ergonomics so they can achieve their goals without Middleware.
784	
785	The term “middleware” often confuses users with Express.js middleware, which can encourage misuse. To clarify our direction, we are renaming the file convention to “proxy.” This highlights that we are moving away from Middleware, breaking down its overloaded features, and making the Proxy clear in its purpose.
786	
787	Next.js provides a codemod to migrate from `middleware.ts` to `proxy.ts`. You can run the following command to migrate:

798	- export function middleware() {
799	+ export function proxy() {
800	```

Everything's built, tested end-to-end, and left uncommitted on `main` (not committing/pushing per default — say the word if you want it committed).

## What I picked, and why

Searched current comparisons (Better Auth vs Auth.js/NextAuth v5 vs Clerk, 2026). Auth.js is in maintenance mode — its own docs now redirect to a Better Auth migration guide. Clerk is a paid hosted service, unnecessary here. **Better Auth** is the standard pick now for self-hosted Next.js: owns the user table in your own DB, TypeScript-first, built-in email/password + OAuth.

Sources: [makerkit.dev](https://makerkit.dev/blog/tutorials/better-auth-vs-clerk), [supastarter.dev](https://supastarter.dev/blog/better-auth-vs-nextauth-vs-clerk), [blog.logrocket.com](https://blog.logrocket.com/best-auth-library-nextjs-2026/), [better-auth.com](https://better-auth.com/docs/integrations/next)

## What I built

- **`src/lib/auth.ts`** — Better Auth server config: email/password + Google OAuth, backed by a local SQLite file (`data/notely.db` via `better-sqlite3` — no external service needed for this scaffold).
- **`src/app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts`** — the auth API (sign up/in/out, OAuth callback, sessions).
- **`src/lib/auth-client.ts`** — browser client for the forms.
- **`src/app/sign-in/`, `src/app/sign-up/`** — pages with email/password form + "Continue with Google" button.
- **`src/lib/users.ts`** — rewired: `listUsers`/`getUser` now read Better Auth's real `user` table instead of the hardcoded array; `getCurrentUser` reads the actual session cookie. Same `User` type and function signatures, so nothing else had to change.
- **`src/app/dashboard/page.tsx`** — now redirects to `/sign-in` if there's no real session, plus a sign-out button.
- **`src/proxy.ts`** — this Next.js version renamed `middleware.ts`→`proxy.ts` (caught via build error, verified against `node_modules/next/dist/docs`); does an optimistic cookie check to redirect signed-out visitors before render.
